claim: When an affordance is revealed on hover-or-focus, track hover and focus as two separate flags, because one shared flag lets a mouse leaving the region erase the hint that only the keyboard user still needs.
because: Landed and verified this round in QuestionnaireStackedOptions: onMouseLeave and onBlur both wrote a single `focused` state, so moving the mouse away hid the 1-9 hotkey badges while keyboard focus was still inside the picker — i.e. the affordance disappeared for exactly the input modality it was built to teach. The component's own docblock named that purpose, which is what made the inversion legible. Fix was `hovered || focused`. No nearest subject: this repo's map does not join this context to a UI-interaction subject.

claim: When a readiness gate offers a manual fallback for an unmet requirement, the fallback's value must not be what clears the gate, because the escape hatch then satisfies the check it was created to bypass.
because: Found (not landed — the fix is outside this worker's paths) in two independent consumers of one blocked-question set: a free-text box is rendered specifically under the missing-credential branch, and both readiness counters subtract any answered question, so typing one character turns a blocked template green. Offered as a sharpening of readiness-prerequisites' existing 'degraded adoption is legitimate, silent degradation is not' rule: the corpus states the two conditions (declared, durable) but does not name this mechanism, where the degradation path and the gate share a single field.

claim: When a reset is keyed on a lifecycle identifier that goes empty -> value at submission, key it on the RETURN to empty instead, because the id changes at the START of the operation and the reset then erases the very state the submission carried.
because: usePersonaCore reset on the build-session id; that id is minted at launch, so the persona core cleared at the instant the intent shipped with its directives and the locked build panel then displayed 'unconfigured' for the whole run. Fixed, and proved by removing the guard and watching the new test go red.

claim: Derive 'the user has configured this' from equality with the default state, never from a latch set on first interaction, because a latch cannot come back down and keeps injecting defaults the user has explicitly cleared.
because: A latched `configured` flag meant toggling a trait on and off left the badge reading 'Custom core' and still appended a default disposition + model tier into the user's prompt. Replaced with a field-wise comparison against DEFAULT_CORE; seeding the old latch back reproduced the failure exactly.

claim: When one item pair can satisfy two conflict classifiers, order them by semantic decisiveness rather than by score — an explicit contradiction signal settles the kind BEFORE any similarity threshold is consulted, because negation is a one-token edit and every similarity measure therefore scores a real contradiction as a near-duplicate.
because: Measured and fixed in this run. detectConflicts ran its duplicate branch first and short-circuited, so 4 of 4 tested negation families ('always/never', 'enable/disable', 'allow/deny', 'should/should not') were classified as duplicates — and 'duplicate' was the only kind whose UI offered a Merge that concatenates both bodies, i.e. the recommended action on two opposite standing instructions was to fuse them into one memory asserting both. The relationship is structural, not incidental: the sharper the contradiction, the higher its textual similarity, so score-ordered classification is guaranteed to lose exactly the contradictions that matter most. Fail-before/pass-after proven by a new test; reordering the two branches fixed all four cases with no change to any threshold. The subject's consolidation technique covers supersedence, the directional measure and states-vs-events, but says nothing about adjudication ORDER between competing classifiers.

claim: A ratcheting baseline that fails on a DROP as well as a rise makes every conformance fix a two-part change — the fix plus the re-baseline — so any worker who can edit code but not the baseline can only fix violations the ratchet does not count, and the gate quietly redirects improvement away from precisely the conditions it was built to name.
because: Measured across this round. 20 census rules match this one context; four separate correct fixes were blocked by the ratchet in BOTH directions — adding aria-expanded to a disclosure control and converting a hand-painted modal to BaseModal would each have DROPPED a baseline, while a document keydown listener and a hand-rolled outside-click each RAISED one. The two rises were genuinely useful signals (they pointed at the repo's own AppKeyboardProvider and useClickOutside primitives, and both fixes were re-done correctly through them), but the two drops converted a landable S fix into backlog with no defect involved. The asymmetry is the lesson: a rise is information, a drop is a coordination cost, and a gate that treats them identically taxes the improvement it exists to encourage.

claim: When a strip of pairwise deltas is built from a bounded fetch window, emit no delta for the window's FIRST element unless the window is provably the whole history — its baseline fell outside the window, so the 'first ever' rule and the 'first fetched' case are indistinguishable at the call site and the fallback always renders the whole set as new.
because: useRunDiffSummaries caps its fan-out at 12 runs and then applied the first-in-history rule to the first run in the WINDOW, so on every team with more than 12 runs the oldest visible timeline marker asserted a false '+N added, 0 removed'. Fixed and verified this round; diff-honesty covers disclosing truncation on the output but not this poisoned-head case in a sequence of diffs.

claim: A latest-wins stale-response guard must cover the APPEND path of a paged list, not only the replace path: load-more computes its offset from the list it is about to append to, so a concurrent filter refresh turns an append into duplicate rows or rows from the previous filter — a corruption the replace-path guard cannot see.
because: useTeamMemories guarded nothing at all; adding createLatestWins to refresh() alone would have left onLoadMore able to append a page computed against an offset the list no longer had. Both paths now share one token sequence. computation-offload states request identity for a diff computation but not the pagination-append variant, where the stale request also carries a stale INPUT (the offset), not just a stale answer.

claim: When a comparison surface aggregates results by a label, verify the label is derived from the compared PARAMETERS and not from the slot's position or creation order — because a positional label makes every ranking a histogram of chance that no downstream significance test can rescue.
because: This context's strategy leaderboard groups by `strategy_label`, which the client assigns positionally as Alpha/Beta/Gamma/Delta while the genes that constitute the strategy are drawn at random per slot — so 'Alpha wins 43%' means 'slot 0 won 43%'. The corpus's `tested-superiority-claims` covers everything downstream of the comparison (test it, correct the family, print only what the evidence supports) but assumes the grouping key already carries the identity being compared. It does not cover the upstream failure where the key is a coincidence of ordering. The bug is also self-confounding here: on a rematch only slot 0 is seeded from the previous winner, so the positional label the leaderboard ranks is systematically advantaged on exactly the runs the user cares about.

claim: When a repo's lint config disables no-undef for TypeScript, treat a scoped lint pass as no evidence that an edit compiles — an inserted helper call whose import was not inserted with it produces zero lint findings, so any automated edit that adds a call must assert the type-checker rather than the linter.
because: An earlier uncommitted round in this exact context added `useRef(0)` and `silentCatch(...)(err)` to CompetitionList.tsx and never added either import. ESLint over all 20 context files reported 0 messages across 20 visited files (verified with -f json, so it was not a no-op run) while `tsc --noEmit` reported two TS2304 errors in that file — and those were 2 of only 3 errors in the entire repository. The failure mode is silent, survives commit, and is invisible to the fast gate a parallel worker is most likely to run because the slow one costs four minutes. I fixed and verified it this round (2 errors -> 0). Filed against `multi-project` (engineering-process/standards-and-gates) as the nearest home for a gate-coverage rule; it is not a natural fit for any existing technique there.

claim: When a texture or pattern vocabulary exists to encode a categorical distinction WITHOUT colour, and the shapes it fills are themselves rotated per category, counter-rotate the pattern by each element's own rotation — because userSpaceOnUse resolves the tile in the referencing element's rotated user space, so orientation-bearing textures silently collapse into duplicate pairs and the accessibility affordance fails while looking correct.
because: Measured in this round: eight textures referenced from eight petals at 45-degree increments collapsed to six distinct renderings — vertical-at-45 and forward-diagonal-at-90 both land at 135 degrees, grid-at-180 and cross-hatch-at-225 both land on the same orthogonal grid. Derived geometrically, then fixed with patternTransform and pinned by a test that was red before the change and green after.

claim: When a repo ratchets its violation counts with a baseline that fails on a DROP as well as a rise, an agent working under a no-shared-files constraint must classify every candidate fix by whether it reduces a counted violation, and demote those to backlog — because a correct fix that lowers a baselined count fails the gate exactly like a regression, and the only remedy (re-baselining) lives in the very file the constraint forbids.
because: Four findings this round were demoted for exactly this reason rather than on their own merits, and the demotion was invisible until I read scripts/census/rules.json instead of running the gate. Not earned by a landed fix, so this is a weaker lead than the first — filed because it changed four routing decisions.

claim: When reduced motion is enforced through CSS (animation-duration zeroing, scroll-behavior overrides), treat imperative motion as uncovered by construction: a Web Animations API animation and an explicit scrollIntoView({behavior:'smooth'}) argument are both unreachable from a stylesheet, so every module that animates imperatively must read the preference signal itself — and a CSS-only audit will report those surfaces as compliant.
because: This round found a spotlight that animated and smooth-scrolled for users with both the OS preference AND the app's own Reduce-motion setting on, inside a codebase whose global CSS handles reduced motion thoroughly and whose shared hook exists. The fail-before test proved the CSS override did not reach either motion. The subject already says 'centralize the signal'; what it does not say is that the usual centralization mechanism has two blind spots that look identical to compliance.

claim: Distinguish a lookup miss on a TOKEN from a miss on CONTENT: rendering the identifier is an honest degradation for a token (a neighbouring label supplies the meaning) but never for content (a title, a body, the reason a record exists) — there the identifier IS the whole card, so omit the record, instrument the miss, and pair the omission with a real empty state so the surface degrades to honest emptiness rather than a wall of markers.
because: Landed this round: a roadmap whose per-item title fell back to the literal `[roadmap.<id>]` on both the live and the bundled path, in a file that had the displayability predicate already written but applied only as an all-or-nothing question about the live payload. The repo's own history records the same marker (`[0.0.2.21]`) reaching every user once before. Filtering created a new failure mode — a blank surface — which is why the empty state is part of the rule and not a separate one.

nearest: none-read-this-round (caching/async-data subject not consulted; novelty NOT verified against the corpus)
claim: When a cache exposes an invalidate entry point, every in-flight request must carry an identity token checked at settle time, because dropping only the cached value leaves the pre-invalidation request both awaitable by the next caller and able to write its stale result back — so the forced refetch serves exactly the data that was invalidated.
because: Landed and probe-verified in staleWhileRevalidate.ts this round: the fail-before run failed 2 of 4 new tests, including one proving the refetch returned the invalidated value. The same token also fixed a second latent bug the naive fix would have introduced — an unguarded .finally on the disowned request evicting a NEWER request from the in-flight map. Confidence held low because bar 3 is unmet: the governing subject I read this round was motion, not a caching subject, so I cannot claim this is novel against the corpus.

nearest: none-read-this-round (type-safety/vocabulary subject not consulted; novelty NOT verified against the corpus)
claim: When one hand-written map doubles as the enumeration of a domain vocabulary, gate it with `satisfies Record<DomainUnion, …>` and derive the enumeration from it, because `Object.keys(map) as Domain[]` is an assertion that erases the only signal capable of reporting that the map has fallen behind the union.
because: Two fixes landed this round on the same shape, each proven by seeding a missing member and watching the compiler name it: the trigger taxonomy (a new TriggerKind silently fell into the 'manual' fallback, in a file whose own header claimed totality for three sibling maps) and ALL_MEMORY_CATEGORIES (the app's memory-category list derived from a colour table and cast into the domain type). Two independent instances in one 17-file context is what raises this above an anecdote; novelty against the corpus is still unverified.

claim: When an eviction loop pops its victim only as a side effect of the disposal function, make the queue's own removal unconditional — because a disposer that early-returns on an unknown id never advances the queue head, turning a stale entry into an infinite loop inside a teardown path.
because: Measured in this run: fleetTerminalManager's `while (parked.length > MAX_PARKED)` relied on disposeTerminal to unpark its victim, and disposeTerminal returns early for an id with no registry entry BEFORE unparking. Reverting the fix hung the test runner past a 120-second wall-clock timeout — a synchronous infinite loop on the UI thread, reached from a plain detach. The technique specifies eviction POLICY (least-recently-viewed, focused-unevictable, eviction-is-a-normal-detach) but says nothing about the eviction loop terminating, and the natural implementation — let the reaper do the removal — is the one that does not.

claim: When you cache the last size pushed to the child to skip no-op resizes, clear that cache on detach — because the next attach may land in a slot with identical dimensions but a child that has been told nothing since, and a suppressed reconciliation there is a permanently mis-sized terminal.
because: Implementing the technique's own no-op-skip rule in this file produced the trap immediately: a naive lastCols/lastRows cache that survives detach makes the second attach into identically-sized geometry push nothing. The technique states both halves separately ('skip the no-ops' and 'reconciling size is an attach-time step') without noting that the first silently defeats the second unless the cache is attach-scoped. I added a dedicated test ('re-reconciles the size on a fresh attach even into identical geometry') because the obvious implementation passes every other test.

claim: When tab panels stay mounted and are hidden with opacity plus pointer-events-none, mark the inactive ones `inert` and `aria-hidden` — because pointer-events-none is a mouse-only guard and keyboard focus and screen readers still walk into the invisible panel's inputs.
because: Earned on VectorKbModal: the modal keeps every visited tab mounted so state survives switching, hiding inactive panels with opacity-0 + pointer-events-none. Tab from the tab bar landed in the hidden Search input and the hidden schema editor's text fields. Adding inert (plus the WAI-ARIA tabs roles) fixed it; tsc and eslint green. The keep-mounted-for-state pattern is stack-independent and the mouse-only nature of pointer-events-none is a property of CSS, not of this repo.

claim: When a shared primitive is disabled app-wide, delete it rather than leaving a null-rendering compatibility shim — because callers keep writing `busy ? <Shim/> : <Icon/>`, which compiles, reads correctly, and ships an empty slot, whereas a removed export fails the build at every site that needs revisiting.
because: Earned on IngestProgressBar: feedback/LoadingSpinner is a deliberate shim that renders null and ignores className, emitting an sr-only status only when passed a `label` no caller passed. Two call sites in this context therefore had no visible indicator AND no screen-reader announcement — the shim delivered neither of the two things it stands in for. Removing them and rendering a real glyph plus role=status/aria-live fixed it. The repo already has a 50-file/68-match census rule chasing this shape after the fact, which is the cost of the shim made visible.

claim: When you introduce a null-aware replacement for a null-blind primitive, ship a gate with it in the same change — because the remaining un-migrated call sites are exactly where the lie survives, and a doc comment naming the anti-pattern enforces nothing.
because: evalFramework.ts:97-99 documents the `compositeScore(x ?? 0, ...)` pattern as the thing compositeScoreFromRow exists to replace. Every other call site in the repo had migrated; two had not, and they were the ones rendering a per-scenario A/B comparison, where a null dimension scored 0/100 and could flip the declared winner. Landed and verified this round (CompareResultsTable.tsx:87-88). The corpus's nullable-cost-never-zero covers what to STORE; nothing covers the migration's tail.

claim: When a save helper converts a rejection into a returned error field instead of rejecting, it degrades to a silent no-op in every consumer that forgets to render that field — so return a discriminated result the caller cannot ignore, or keep rejecting.
because: useAppSetting.save() catches, logs and parks the message on `error`; ProviderCredentialField never read it, so a failed write of an API key produced no toast, no message and no visible state change — the user leaves believing the credential is stored. The optional-field shape is what made the omission invisible: the code compiles, lints clean, and looks complete. Fixed and verified this round. The corpus's failure-not-empty-success law states that failure must surface; this names the specific API shape that reliably prevents it.

claim: When a summary tile sits directly above the itemized list of the same thing, pin both to the same COLLECTION, not merely the same predicate — a merged or unified view makes the set the variable while the rule looks identical, so the two paths pass every review and still disagree.
because: TraceSummary folded trace.spans (backend) while TraceInspector listed cards from unifiedTrace.spans (frontend pipeline spans merged in). Both applied 'a span with an error', so a reviewer of either path saw the correct rule; a run that failed at frontend validation still printed '0 errors' with the error card rendered beneath it. Fixed by computing the set once in the caller and passing the count; the summary now states no rule at all.

claim: When a surface seeds a placeholder for data an agent or a later process will supply, the placeholder may describe the SHAPE of the work but must never carry a completed or succeeded state — because a progress rollup computed over it is indistinguishable from real progress, and because an always-seeded placeholder makes the surface's own empty state unreachable, so that state ships unreviewed.
because: Studio's MOCK_PHASES shipped two of six phases as `done` and one as `active`, with notes describing one specific portfolio site, for every project regardless of its stated vision. The plan button read '2/6' before a single file existed. The second half of the rule is the part that surprised me: because the placeholder was seeded on every creation path, the drawer's careful 'No plan yet — Athena will lay one out as you build' empty state (with its own motion-traced glyph) could never render in practice. I changed the seed to all-pending, pinned it with a test, and proved the guard bites by seeding the old value back.

claim: When a host page receives postMessage reports from frames it embeds, authenticate the reporting frame by contentWindow identity, never by a self-declared field in the payload — the window message event fires for every frame on the page including anything the embedded document itself embeds, so a `source: 'our-agent'` marker is a string any nested frame can copy.
because: Studio's preview handler gated on `d.source === 'athena-agent'` for both of its message kinds. One branch happened to resolve the reporting frame by contentWindow (it needed the tab id) and was therefore accidentally safe; the sibling branch did not, and would move a global UI element to a rectangle supplied by any nested frame in a user-authored dev site. The same guard was one line away in the same handler and had simply not been generalised — which is what makes this a rule worth stating rather than a bug worth fixing.

claim: When a client coalesces reads from many independent callers into one bulk request, it must enforce the backend's batch ceiling itself by chunking, because the per-call-site bound that made the ceiling unreachable ceases to exist the moment an aggregator sits in front of it — and the overflow fails the whole batch, so unrelated readers all resolve to 'absent' at once.
because: Measured this run: the settings coalescer aggregated every same-tick read into one get_app_settings_bulk with no size awareness, while the backend hard-rejects >256 keys with a Validation error, and the coalescer's documented rejection fan-out then failed every waiter. A fail-before test with 296 keys reproduced it; chunking at the ceiling fixed it and made a single bad chunk fail only its own waiters.

claim: An effect's dependency list is the identity of the session it starts, so caller-supplied callbacks must never appear in it — latch them in refs and key only on the values that name the session; if the effect drives a poll whose result sets state, a callback in the deps makes the restart self-sustaining and the loop runs at network speed instead of at the configured interval.
because: Measured this run: a polling hook depended on nine caller callbacks; one consumer was constructed with an inline arrow, so every render restarted the effect — clearing the timer, resetting the backoff and the consecutive-failure counter (making the session-lost path unreachable), and re-polling immediately, while the poll's own onLines state write triggered the next render. A fail-before test showed 6 polls where 1 was due.

claim: When one confirm-then-execute guard serves several statements authored on the same surface, bind the pending statement to its execution target when it is stashed (or drop it when the target changes), because a guard keyed only on the connection cannot see the target swap and will report the confirmed statement's result against the wrong author.
because: Landed and verified in ChatTab: the shared safe-mode hook's drift guard compares the runQuery identity, which is bound to credentialId alone, while the message the result is written to lives in a ref that every Run press re-points. Stash a mutation on message A, run a read on B, confirm: A executed and A's rows appeared under B. The guard was working exactly as designed and still could not see it.

claim: A result surface that can be re-run in place must clear the previous result when the new run fails, because an error rendered above stale rows reads as that error's output and is indistinguishable from a partial success.
because: Landed and verified in ChatTab with a fail-before probe: the catch set the error field and left the result field, so AssistantSqlBlock painted the previous run's grid directly under a fresh engine error. result-fidelity names the zero-rows/error pair but not the stale-success/error pair, which only exists once a statement is re-runnable in place.

claim: When a locale catalogue holds a key whose source-language value appears verbatim as a string literal in the code, treat it as a wiring bug rather than a duplicate, because it means the key was minted and translated for that exact site and never referenced — a state no coverage gate can see, since the catalogues are complete and the literal is syntactically valid.
because: Found and fixed three of them in one 244-line file: db.query_generated, db.query_failed and db.cancelled exist in en.json and all 13 locales (spot-checked cs/ja/ar) and are referenced nowhere in 4,900 files, while ChatTab rendered the identical English literals. Both of this repo's i18n gates were green throughout: the strict coverage check compares catalogues to each other, and the hardcoded-JSX lint rule does not see a string in an object-property position. The detection is a cheap join of catalogue values against source literals.

claim: When a patch/overlay document merges into a canonical one, an EMPTY collection in the patch must mean 'not mentioned', never 'delete' — because `[].every(p)` is vacuously true, so the wholesale-replace branch guarded by it erases exactly the structure the patch format promised it could not touch.
because: Measured and fixed in this round: a strings-only translation overlay writing "use_cases": [] replaced the canonical list with [], defeating the module's own stated contract that structural fields stay single-sourced in the canonical file — and defeating it AFTER the checksum that protects the canonical had already passed, so no integrity layer could see it. Fail-before proven by removing the guard; the test goes red.

claim: When an adapter OVERWRITES the shared pipeline's output after the pipeline has run, it silently opts out of every guarantee the pipeline enforces — so either the override runs before the waist, or the override must re-apply them explicitly.
because: Earned in this round: sanitizing at the waist covered three of four adapters, and the GitHub Actions adapter then rewrote identity, instructions, summary and full_prompt_markdown from raw source fields — reintroducing the exact prompt-injection path the waist had just closed, in the one adapter that looked most carefully written. The intermediate-representation technique says adapters lower INTO the IR and says nothing about adapters mutating it afterwards, which is how the hole stayed invisible.

claim: When a build-time static analyzer forces one hand-written copy of an enumeration that has a single source of truth elsewhere (a bundler glob, a macro list), derive every other copy from the source and add a source-text assertion over the unavoidable one — because a missing entry there fails OPEN: the feature silently never loads, with no runtime error to notice.
because: Earned in this round: three copies of the locale list existed (a regex, a Vite glob, and a test that re-typed the same 13 codes), and the manifest they should all derive from asserts in its own header that 'no other file references a locale by code'. Two copies were replaced with derivations; the glob cannot be derived because Vite analyses it statically, so a test now reads the source text and fails when a manifest locale has no pattern. Fail-before proven by deleting one glob line.

claim: When a verdict is widened from a boolean to a named state, retire the boolean in the same change -- a back-compat boolean derived from the new enum IS the collapse the widening was meant to prevent, and every surface still reading it silently re-manufactures the old two-state answer.
because: Personas widened its credential healthcheck to HealthProbeState{Verified,Unverifiable,Failed} and kept success = (state != Failed) for back-compat. Unknown therefore reads TRUE. The badge renderer migrated to the enum; the result panel next to it kept branching on success and painted an unverifiable probe emerald with a check mark -- the exact green claim the third state was introduced to stop. Neither the type checker nor the census rule written for this defect class saw it, because both were watching the type boundary while the collapse happened at the render.

claim: When a client app lazy-loads routes, make the route registry a single `satisfies Record<AllSections, LazyRoute>` map so an un-lazy addition is a typecheck failure, because convention-level lazy discipline dies by one static import - here a single static overlay import silently made 890KB of vendor JS eager while every documented route stayed lazy
because: 2026-08-30 architect run measured the eager closure: sectionRouter typed registry held for 10 routes/19 overlays, the one surface added outside it (App.tsx static LiveChannelOverlay import) dragged markdown+chart vendors eager; fix + codification landed (commits d27d7d885, c49344551)

claim: when a pipeline stamps a generated character/self document, the stamp must be write-only-if-absent - any rebuild that re-stamps unconditionally overwrites the operator's authored identity behind a green build
because: personas' promote/adopt raw-UPDATEd core_profile unconditionally; the living-agent rebase had to convert both sites to seed-if-absent or the new Core editor's writes would die on the next rebuild

claim: when an autonomous cycle's refusals are frequent and identical, dedupe the durable refusal record to one per reason-kind per period while narrating every tick in logs - a refusal ledger that grows per tick trains the operator to ignore it
because: the persona attention loop at a 300s tick with a 30-min floor would write ~240 identical interval_floor rows/day/persona; deduped to one per reason-kind per UTC day with per-tick tracing, accepted on measured evidence

claim: when a file's tail hosts a feature-gated test module, tests appended at file end silently join it and never run under the default feature set - assert a new test RAN (count it), never just that the suite is green
because: WP4's memory-door tests landed inside an ml-gated vec_tests tail module and executed zero times while every gate read green; caught only because the builder counted its own test runs

claim: When a self-model document gains a second, operator-only author, refuse the agent's diffs at BOTH the propose and the apply door, not just at apply, because a proposal that can never be applied still reaches a human inbox and reads as a legitimate request.
because: Shipped a two-author manifest (operator law sections + agent self-model sections) and found that guarding only the apply door let refused-by-design proposals accumulate in the review queue; guarding propose as well made the refusal legible at the moment it was earned.

claim: A memory dashboard must distinguish an unmeasured value from a measured zero at every tile, and the distinction has to survive into the type: model the count as nullable rather than defaulting a lookup miss to 0.
because: The coverage tile's whole purpose is showing what the brain holds nothing about; a `counts.get(id) ?? 0` rendered never-measured charters as a confident 0 and a repo lint caught it. Making the field nullable forced every consumer to state which case it was drawing.

claim: When a spring/follow-value hook is fed a plain number instead of a motion value, push every new target through .set() in an effect, because the library reads a number once at attach time and a re-render with a new number never moves the animation.
because: framer-motion 12 useSpring(number) in a polled status gauge: motion-dom attachFollow subscribes only to MotionValue sources, so both the arc and the counter stayed at the first poll's value for the life of the view; a render test went red on the old code and green after spring.set() (commit 7c45a4f2c).

claim: When a string needs a control character as a field separator, write it as an escape sequence rather than a raw byte, because one raw NUL makes grep report the whole file as binary and git render every diff of it as Bin, so the file drops out of code search and review while still compiling.
because: useHealthCheck.ts carried two raw 0x00 bytes in a template literal; grep -n over the file returned zero lines for any pattern and four commits touching it showed as Bin in git stat; escapes restored 507 addressable lines with identical hashes (pinned by test)

claim: When an undo entry's restore persists through I/O, it must reject on failure even after reporting it to the user, because the history store decides success from the promise and a swallowed failure moves the entry to redo and loses it.
because: personas-desktop useEditorSave: restore toasted and returned; EditorDocument.undo() filed the entry as undone, canUndo went false, disk kept the value; fixed by rethrow, hook test red-then-green
